issues.description: verifyToken returns null on failure instead of throwing, so requireUser sets req.user = null and calls next(), letting unauthenticated requests through to handlers that then crash on req.user.id; the raw Authorization header, possibly with a 'Bearer ' prefix, is also passed to jwt.verify.
Async route handler has no error handling, so a rejection (for example a missing password or a DB error) becomes an unhandled promise rejection and the request hangs under Express 4.
The cart, including priceCents, is taken from the client request body and used to compute the charge, allowing price tampering, and there is no input validation.
The sales report route requires only a logged-in user with no role check, so any customer can read staff sales data.
The admin user-deletion route has neither authentication nor an admin authorization check, so anyone can delete users.
SQL injection: the email is concatenated directly into the query string instead of using a parameter.
Passwords are hashed with unsalted MD5, which is trivially crackable; use bcrypt, scrypt or argon2.
expiresIn is given the number 30, which jsonwebtoken interprets as seconds, so tokens expire after 30 seconds instead of 30 minutes.
jwt.verify does not restrict the accepted algorithms; pass an explicit algorithms option.

The cart-full check runs before checking whether the SKU already exists, so adding to an existing line fails when the cart is full; quantity is also not validated (negative or non-integer values accepted).
JWT_SECRET and DATABASE_URL are not validated at startup, so a missing secret only fails later at signing time.
The connection is released only on success; if connection.query throws, the client leaks and the pool will eventually be exhausted (use try/finally or pool.query).
query() returns an object { rows, rowCount }, not an array, so array destructuring `const [row]` throws a TypeError; use `const { rows }`.
The check-then-update on stock is not atomic and not in a transaction, so concurrent orders can oversell; use a single conditional UPDATE.
The UPDATE query is not awaited, so the function returns before the stock is decremented and any error becomes an unhandled rejection.
user.name is interpolated into HTML without escaping, allowing HTML injection in emails.
formatCurrency arguments are swapped (currency first, amount second), producing a wrong string such as 'NaN 12345'.
The empty catch block silently swallows email send failures with no logging.
config.taxRate does not exist (config defines vatRate), so the tax is NaN.
Off-by-one loop condition `i <= cart.items.length` accesses an undefined item on the last iteration and throws a TypeError, so every order fails.
The total in integer cents is passed to chargeCard, which expects euros and multiplies by 100, so customers are charged 100 times the amount.
Stock reservation, charge and order insert are not transactional, so a failure after reserving or charging leaves stock reserved or the card charged with no order and no refund or rollback.
The full card number and CVC are written to the logs, a PCI-DSS violation and sensitive data exposure.
The amount is treated as euros and multiplied by 100, which is inconsistent with the integer-cents convention used by the callers.
refundCharge swallows all errors and returns true, so failed refunds are reported as successful.
SQL injection: the from and to query parameters are concatenated into the SQL string.
The empty catch hides database errors and returns an empty report, masking failures as no sales.
SQL injection: the email is concatenated into the query instead of being passed as a parameter.
Off-by-one error: slice(start, start + pageSize - 1) returns only pageSize-1 items per page.
